name: Provocative Artifacts
description:
Provocative artefacts are deliberately designed objects or representations intended to elicit reflection, discussion or reaction rather than simply demonstrate a solution. By embodying an unusual, uncomfortable or exaggerated proposition, the artefact can make assumptions and values easier to examine.

The responses it produces can become material for design research or critical inquiry.
whenToUse: Use provocative artefacts when direct questioning is unlikely to expose assumptions or when a tangible proposition can help participants engage with abstract, contested or future-oriented issues.
steps: Identify the assumption or issue to investigate.
Decide what kind of response would be useful to elicit.
Develop a proposition that makes the issue tangible.
Create an artefact with enough coherence to be interpreted.
Introduce it with an appropriate amount of context.
Ask participants to explain their interpretations and concerns.
Analyse the discussion rather than treating reactions as simple approval or rejection.
lookOutFor: Provocation should serve an inquiry rather than exist only to shock.
Consider emotional consequences for participants before introducing disturbing material.
Participants may interpret the artefact very differently from the designer's intention; those differences are often important rather than errors to correct.

resources.citation: Gaver, W. (2012). “What Should We Expect from Research Through Design?” *CHI 2012*.
Dunne, A. & Raby, F. (2013). *Speculative Everything*. MIT Press.
